title: Print Culture and the Modern World

topics.title: The first printed books: East Asia and Europe

learn.hook: Before printing, every single book was copied by hand. One Bible could take months! Then woodblocks and a clever German goldsmith changed everything.
points: The earliest print technology came from China, Japan and Korea. From about AD 594, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks. Since only one side of the thin paper could be printed, it was folded and stitched into an 'accordion book'. For a long time the imperial state was the biggest producer of printed material, such as textbooks for the civil service examination.

Buddhist missionaries from China brought hand printing to Japan around AD 768-770. The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, with six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

Marco Polo returned to Italy from China in 1295 with knowledge of woodblock printing. Paper reached Europe through the silk route. Earlier, luxury editions were handwritten on vellum, a parchment made from animal skin.

Johann Gutenberg, who grew up seeing wine and olive presses and later learnt to polish stones and make lead moulds, perfected his printing system by 1448. The first book he printed was the Bible: about 180 copies, which took three years to produce.
Between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe. This 'print revolution' made books cheaper and created a new reading public in place of a mainly 'hearing public'.

example.q: Think it through: How did the printing press change who could read books?
steps: Hand-copying was slow and costly, so books were few and expensive.
The press could print many copies quickly, so the time and cost of each book fell sharply.
Cheaper books reached markets and many more people could buy them.
So reading spread beyond the elite, and a new reading public was born.
example.answer: It made books faster and cheaper to produce, so many more ordinary people could buy and read them.

learn.reallife: When your school prints hundreds of copies of a question paper in a few minutes, it is using the great-great-grandchildren of Gutenberg's press.

quiz.q: Which country developed the earliest kind of print technology?
quiz.explain: China, along with Japan and Korea, had the earliest print technology, using hand printing from woodblocks.

quiz.q: Why were traditional Chinese books folded into 'accordion books'?
options: Only one side of the thin, porous paper could be printed
Ink was too costly to use on a full page
Paper was too thick to cut
quiz.explain: Because both sides could not be printed, the printed sheets were folded and stitched at the side.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the word 'accordion' instead of the reason

quiz.q: What is the oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868?
quiz.explain: The Diamond Sutra had six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with famous books from Europe or India

quiz.q: Who brought the knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy?
quiz.explain: The explorer Marco Polo returned to Italy in 1295 with this knowledge.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Gutenberg learnt printing directly from China

quiz.q: What was vellum?
options: A parchment made from the skin of animals
quiz.explain: Vellum was used for luxury handwritten editions for aristocrats and rich libraries.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term

quiz.q: Which of these experiences helped Gutenberg design his printing press?
options: Working in a Chinese imperial printing office
Seeing wine and olive presses on the estate where he grew up
Building steam engines with James Watt
quiz.explain: He adapted the idea of the screw press used for olives and grapes, and used his skill in making lead moulds for letters.
quiz.mistake: Links Gutenberg with people from a different time or place

quiz.q: About how many copies of the Bible did Gutenberg print, taking three years?
quiz.explain: About 180 copies were printed. Later, presses across Europe produced millions of books.
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with later, much larger print numbers

quiz.q: What is meant by the 'print revolution'?
options: The ban on printing in Europe
A war fought over printing presses
The spread of printing that made books cheap and created a new reading public
quiz.explain: Between 1450 and 1550 presses spread across Europe, changing how people got information and knowledge.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'revolution' to mean a political uprising

learn.hook: India already had beautiful handwritten manuscripts on palm leaves. Then a ship to Goa brought a strange new machine: the printing press.
points: India had a rich tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and many vernacular languages, written on palm leaves or handmade paper. They were costly and fragile, so they were not widely used in everyday life.

The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani, and by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kannada languages.

Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book. By 1710, Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts, many of them translations of older works.

In 1780 James Augustus Hickey began editing the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine. He published advertisements and also gossip about the Company's senior officials. Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted him and encouraged officially approved newspapers.
The first Indian newspaper to appear was the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Warren Hastings act against Hickey?
steps: Hickey's paper published gossip about the Company's senior officials in India.
Such reports could damage the image of the colonial government.
Hastings wanted to control what was printed about British rule.
So he persecuted Hickey and encouraged newspapers that would protect the government's image.
example.answer: Hickey's paper criticised and gossiped about Company officials, so Hastings tried to silence him and backed approved papers instead.

learn.reallife: Many Indian newspapers today are more than a hundred years old. Their story began in the bustling presses of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

topics.title: Print, reform and revolution in Europe

learn.hook: One monk's list of 95 complaints, printed thousands of times, helped split the Church in Europe. Print had become powerful!
points: Not everyone welcomed print. The Latin scholar and Catholic reformer Erasmus worried that books would spread rebellious and irreligious ideas.

In 1517 the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising many practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Printed copies spread widely, leading to division in the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. Luther said, 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.'
Worried by the spread of new ideas, the Roman Church began keeping an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

By the 17th and 18th centuries literacy grew in Europe. Pedlars sold cheap chapbooks in England, and the Bibliotheque Bleue in France offered low-priced small books. Almanacs, ballads, newspapers and periodicals spread too. The writer Louise-Sebastien Mercier called the printing press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.

Many historians argue that print helped bring about the French Revolution: it popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau, created a culture of dialogue and debate, and spread literature that mocked royalty. In the 19th century Richard M. Hoe of New York perfected the power-driven cylindrical press, which could print 8,000 sheets per hour.

example.q: Think it through: Why did print help the ideas of the Reformation spread so fast?
steps: Before print, a reformer's ideas spread slowly by hand-copied letters and sermons.
Luther's Ninety Five Theses were printed in large numbers and read widely.
People could read and discuss the ideas themselves in many places at once.
So the debate spread quickly, leading to the Protestant Reformation.
example.answer: Print reproduced Luther's writings in large numbers, so many people read and debated them at the same time.

learn.reallife: Today, a post or a video can spread around India in hours. In the 16th century, the printing press did something similar for Luther's ideas.

quiz.q: Why was Erasmus worried about printing?
options: He feared books would spread rebellious and irreligious ideas
He thought books would become too expensive
He had invented a rival machine
He wanted only Chinese books to be printed
quiz.explain: Erasmus, a Catholic reformer, felt that the flood of books could carry harmful ideas to readers.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyone welcomed print

quiz.q: In which year did Martin Luther write the Ninety Five Theses?
quiz.explain: Luther wrote them in 1517. 1448 is Gutenberg's press, 1558 the Index of Prohibited Books and 1789 the French Revolution.
quiz.mistake: Confuses dates related to print in Europe

quiz.q: What did Martin Luther's Ninety Five Theses criticise?
options: Many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church
quiz.explain: His criticism, spread through print, led to the Protestant Reformation.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the subject of the Theses

quiz.q: Which famous line about printing is linked with Martin Luther?
options: When France sneezes, Europe catches cold
The printing press is the most powerful engine of progress
Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one
quiz.explain: Luther praised print. Mercier called the press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Luther's quote with Mercier's

quiz.q: Why did the Roman Church start the Index of Prohibited Books from 1558?
options: To control the spread of books it considered against its teachings
quiz.explain: Faced with new interpretations of faith spreading through print, the Church tried to ban certain books.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Index was a book list for readers' convenience

quiz.q: What were chapbooks?
options: Cheap pocket-sized books sold by pedlars in England
quiz.explain: Pedlars called chapmen sold chapbooks, so even the poor could buy something to read.
quiz.mistake: Confuses chapbooks with luxury books

quiz.q: Which is one way print is said to have helped the French Revolution?
options: It praised the monarchy and made it stronger
It was banned completely in France
It popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau
quiz.explain: Print spread Enlightenment ideas, built a culture of debate and mocked royalty, preparing the ground for revolution.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of print on the monarchy

quiz.q: Richard M. Hoe's power-driven cylindrical press could print how many sheets per hour?
quiz.explain: Hoe's press printed 8,000 sheets per hour, especially useful for newspapers.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall the press's speed

teach.praise: Amazing! Print carried ideas so fast that it shook churches and kings.

learn.hook: In 19th-century India, presses became busy debate halls on paper, where reformers, women writers and workers all found a voice.
points: From the early 19th century, print carried lively debates on religion and society. Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821, while Hindu orthodox groups commissioned the Samachar Chandrika. In 1822 two Persian newspapers, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar, appeared, and in the same year the Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar was published.

The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands of fatwas guiding Muslims in daily life. The first printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in 1810. Presses like the Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published religious texts in vernacular languages, so people could read them easily.

Women became readers and writers. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote Amar Jiban, published in 1876, the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language. In the 1880s Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai in Maharashtra wrote about the hard lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows.

Reformers wrote against caste injustice: Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri (1871); B.R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) in Madras also wrote powerfully on caste. Kashibaba, a Kanpur mill worker, wrote and published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938.

The colonial state tried to control print. After 1857, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, gave the government wide powers to censor the vernacular press. When Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote with sympathy in his paper Kesari about Punjab revolutionaries deported in 1907, he was imprisoned in 1908, sparking widespread protests.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the British pass the Vernacular Press Act in 1878?
steps: After 1857, the colonial government became suspicious of the Indian press.
Vernacular newspapers were becoming more numerous and assertively nationalist.
They criticised colonial policies in languages ordinary Indians could read.
So the Act gave the government power to censor reports and editorials and punish critical papers.
example.answer: Vernacular papers were spreading criticism of colonial rule to ordinary readers, so the government took powers to censor them.

learn.reallife: A free press that reports and debates public issues is part of Indian democracy today, protected by the freedom of speech and expression in our Constitution.

quiz.mistake: Mixes up the languages of the 1822 newspapers

quiz.q: What did the Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, publish in large numbers?
options: Fatwas guiding Muslims in their daily lives
quiz.explain: It published thousands of fatwas explaining the meaning of Islamic teachings for everyday life.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the role of the Deoband Seminary

quiz.q: Why was Rashsundari Debi's 'Amar Jiban' important?
options: It was banned by the Vernacular Press Act
It was the first Tamil book
It was the first newspaper in India
It was the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language
quiz.explain: Published in 1876, it was written by a woman who had learnt to read secretly, showing how print gave women a voice.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up firsts from the history of print in India

quiz.q: Which book did Jyotiba Phule write in 1871 about the injustices of the caste system?
quiz.explain: In Gulamgiri, Phule wrote about caste injustice and linked it with the idea of slavery.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other books in the syllabus

quiz.q: Who wrote and published 'Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal' in 1938?
quiz.explain: Kashibaba wrote about the links between caste and class exploitation, showing that workers too used print.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that workers were writers too

quiz.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was modelled on which laws?
quiz.explain: It was modelled on the Irish Press Laws and gave the government wide powers to censor the vernacular press.
quiz.mistake: Confuses press laws with other laws in the syllabus

quiz.q: Why was Bal Gangadhar Tilak imprisoned in 1908?
options: He printed the first Tamil book
He refused to pay the salt tax
He wrote with sympathy about deported Punjab revolutionaries in his paper Kesari
quiz.explain: His writing in Kesari about the revolutionaries deported in 1907 led to his imprisonment and widespread protests.
quiz.mistake: Links Tilak's arrest with events from a different period
